stories.title: Walmart Closes on Celina Property, 2nd Store on Way
stories.excerpt: A second Walmart is coming to Celina. The company bought 41 acres at the southeast corner of FM 455 and the Dallas North Tollway, adjacent to Legacy Hills in Celina, a substantial master-planned community in Celina. The town is America’s fastest-growing town. Celina City Council approved an economic development agreement with Wal-Mart in July. Walmart is set to receive up to $5.1 million in incentives. The planned store will be at least 150,000 square feet and requires a minimum $25 million investment from Walmart, not including the cost of the land, according to the agreement. Once the store is built, Walmart has to maintain at least 120 full-time employees for the duration of the agreement. The city of Celina and the Celina Economic Development Corp. will each give Walmart a 50% sales tax reimbursement grant for 10 years, It’s the town’s second Walmart. The city’s first Walmart opened off Preston Road in April (shown). The post Walmart Closes on Celina Property, 2nd Store on Way appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Walmart opens 2nd Celina, TX store; 41 acres, $25M+ investment, 150K+ SF
City grants $5.1M incentives; 50% sales tax reimbursement for 10 years
Celina fastest-growing U.S. town; store requires 120+ FT employees
stories.summary: Walmart closed on 41 acres in Celina, Texas (America's fastest-growing town) for its second location, a 150,000+ sq. ft. store requiring a minimum $25 million investment. The city is providing up to $5.1 million in incentives via 50% sales tax reimbursement grants split between the city and economic development corp. over 10 years. Walmart must maintain at least 120 full-time employees for the agreement duration.
stories.impact: Major retail anchor signals strong population inflow to Dallas-Fort Worth exurbs. Celina's rapid growth and Walmart's second entry validate underlying demand fundamentals—multifamily developers should prioritize land acquisition in Celina and adjacent fast-growing suburbs (Frisco, Prosper, McKinney) before retail-driven density and pricing accelerate further. Retail density follows housing demand; early-mover advantage in residential supply is critical.

stories.title: Aarthi Bansidhar Joins Midwood as Chief Financial Officer
stories.excerpt: New York City-based private real estate firm Midwood Investment & Development has hired a new chief financial officer. Aarthi Bansidhar, a former managing director at Madison Capital, joined Midwood in June to lead its financial strategy, capital planning and performance management efforts across its national portfolio of office, residential and retail assets. “Aarthi brings an impressive track record of financial expertise and strategic leadership to the team, which will be invaluable as our company continues to grow and build out our national portfolio,” John Usdan, CEO of Midwood, said in a statement. Bansidhar has worked in finance and real estate for two decades, working at Madison for over 13 years. Before that, she worked as a senior manager of the asset management practice at Ernst & Young for close to nine years, according to her LinkedIn profile. “I’m eager to help strengthen our financial strategy and contribute to the company’s continued growth,” Bansidhar said in a statement. Bansidhar studied business management and accounting at Baruch College. Projects currently under development for Midwood include a 25-unit condominium project at 150 East 78th Street on Manhattan’s Upper East Side in collaboration with Robert A.M. Stern Architects, and a 31-story multifamily rental building at 210 South 12th Street in Philadelphia. Mark Hallum can be reached at mhallum@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Midwood Investment hires CFO Aarthi Bansidhar from Madison Capital
20+ years finance/RE experience; leads strategy across office, residential, retail
Midwood expanding national portfolio; NYC-based firm strengthening capital planning
stories.summary: Midwood Investment & Development, a New York City-based real estate firm, hired Aarthi Bansidhar as CFO in June. Bansidhar, formerly a managing director at Madison Capital with 20 years of finance and real estate experience, will lead financial strategy, capital planning, and performance management across Midwood's national portfolio of office, residential, and retail assets. The hire signals the firm's growth trajectory and intent to scale nationally.
stories.impact: Limited direct impact on multifamily supply or demand. This is a capital-markets signal: Midwood's CFO upgrade and emphasis on "national portfolio expansion" and "financial strategy" suggest the firm is preparing for increased acquisition and development activity, likely positioning for a post-rate-cut capital environment. Monitor Midwood's pipeline for competitive bid situations and market entry signals in secondary metros.

stories.title: Doral Whole Foods-Anchored Retail Center Trades for $83M
stories.excerpt: A Whole Foods-anchored retail center in Doral has sold for $83 million. The recently completed Doral Marketplace was sold by SJC Ventures. The buyer was a group led by Jonathan Perlman. Perlman runs senior living and memory care facilities. Perlman’s company assumed $50.1 million of existing debt assigned to the Bank of Texas. SJC Ventures broke ground on the 10-acre site in 2024 and recently completed the 88,938-square-foot shopping center. This sale did not include the 1.88-acre portion of the property leased to Chick-fil-A. The sales price comes out to just under $1,000 a square foot. The 43,000-square-foot Whole Foods at Doral Marketplace opened earlier this summer. Other tenants include J. Crew, Shake Shack, First Watch, GoodVets, The Spot Barbershop, Encore Nails, Vio MedSpa, and Apizza Brooklyn Resto + Vino. The post Doral Whole Foods-Anchored Retail Center Trades for $83M appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Doral Marketplace trades $83M; Whole Foods-anchored, 88,938 SF, ~$930/SF
SJC Ventures sold; buyer group led by Jonathan Perlman (senior living)
Buyer assumed $50.1M debt from Bank of Texas; newly completed 2024
stories.summary: Doral Marketplace, a newly completed 88,938 sq. ft. Whole Foods-anchored retail center in Doral, Florida, sold for $83 million ($930/sq. ft.). SJC Ventures developed the property (ground broke 2024, recently completed); buyer Jonathan Perlman's group assumed $50.1 million in existing Bank of Texas debt. The sale excludes a 1.88-acre Chick-fil-A pad site.
stories.impact: Minimal direct relevance to multifamily development. However, the transaction signals healthy retail fundamentals and debt availability in South Florida, suggesting strong consumer demand and lender confidence in the Miami-Dade/Doral submarket. The ~$930/SF valuation for a stabilized, anchor-tenanted retail box signals liquidity and demand for mixed-use real estate in the region, which may support feasibility for multifamily-plus-retail developments in Doral.

stories.title: Let’s Do the “Mini” Twist
stories.excerpt: Executive Summary The Treasury Department’s decision to double long-end bond buybacks produced the desired initial market response, but investors should not confuse a successful squeeze on crowded positions with a durable change in the interest rate outlook. The action can reduce the amount of duration the private market must absorb at the margin. In that respect, it carries echoes of Operation Twist. It does not have the scale, monetary transmission or balance-sheet effects of quantitative easing, however, and it cannot offset the fiscal and inflation forces pushing yields higher. The Market Responded Before the Math Mattered Treasury increased the maximum size of liquidity-support buybacks for nominal securities with 10 to 30 years remaining to at least $4 billion per operation from $2 billion. The change takes effect Sept. 9 and remains in place through the Nov. 4 quarterly refunding. Treasury described the move as support for market liquidity, citing the volume of high-quality securities offered during previous operations. Importantly, it did not formally announce a yield target. The market nevertheless interpreted the surprise as an effort to arrest the long-end selloff. The 30-year yield, which reached 5.327% on Aug. 18—its highest level since 2007—fell to about 5.18% after the announcement. The 10-year yield declined by a similar magnitude. That reaction was larger than the program’s cash size alone would justify. Investors had accumulated curve-steepening trades based on the view that fiscal concerns would push 30-year yields higher relative to shorter maturities. The announcement forced traders to unwind those positions, amplifying the rally. The effect quickly weakened. The 30-year yield moved back above 5.22% the next day as investors returned their attention to debt, inflation and supply. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, in an interview on CNBC last Thursday, also said the purchases could be increased again, adding an important policy signal but also ra
bullets: Treasury doubles long-end bond buybacks to $4B from $2B operations
Program targets 10-30 year securities; effect through Nov. 4 refunding
30-year yield fell 5.327% to 5.18% post-announcement; no formal yield target
stories.summary: The U.S. Treasury Department doubled the maximum size of liquidity-support buybacks for long-end securities (10-30 years) to at least $4 billion per operation, effective Sept. 9 through Nov. 4. The move, characterized as "Operation Twist lite," aimed to arrest the long-end bond selloff and reduce duration pressure on the private market. The 30-year yield fell from 5.327% (Aug. 18 high) to ~5.18% following the surprise announcement, though the Treasury declined to formally announce a yield target.
stories.impact: Modest near-term refinancing relief but does not signal a durable shift in rate trajectory. Long-end yields remain elevated; developers relying on fixed-rate permanent financing will see continued pressure on cap rates and debt service costs. This is a liquidity measure, not a monetary pivot. Multifamily construction loans and acquisition financing remain sensitive to sustained 5%+ long-end rates. Underwriting should assume rates do not decline materially; floating-rate cap and refinance risk remains elevated through 2025.

stories.title: FRP, Woodfield Begin Work on Expansive Estero Development
stories.excerpt: FRP Development Corp, in partnership with Woodfield Development, has started construction on the first phase of its Coconut Road mixed-use development in the Village of Estero, Florida. At 23281 Lyden Drive, across from Coconut Point, the development is planned to include approximately 600 apartment homes, 80,000 square feet of retail space, 20,000 square feet of office space and a boutique 190-room hotel. It’s to be designed by Dover Kohl & Partners. Estero is south of Fort Myers. The first phase will include approximately 296 apartment homes in a mix of three- and four-story residential buildings, together with 30,000 square feet of retail space. Initial residential units are anticipated to deliver in the third quarter of 2027. The developers secured an $81.5 million construction loan from Santander Bank to support construction of the project. Construction of the first phase is being led by general contractor Brooks & Freund, in collaboration with Humphreys & Partners Architects and interior design firm ID & Design International. The post FRP, Woodfield Begin Work on Expansive Estero Development appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: FRP & Woodfield break ground Estero, FL mixed-use; 600 apartments planned
Phase 1: 296 units (3-4 story), 30K SF retail; $81.5M construction loan from Santander
Residential delivery Q3 2027; mixed-use includes 190-room hotel, 20K SF office
stories.summary: FRP Development and Woodfield Development began construction on Coconut Road, a 600-unit mixed-use development in the Village of Estero, Florida (south of Fort Myers). Phase 1 includes 296 apartment homes across three- and four-story buildings, 30,000 sq. ft. of retail, with residential delivery anticipated Q3 2027. The developers secured an $81.5 million construction loan from Santander; full build-out includes a 190-room hotel and 20,000 sq. ft. of office space.
stories.impact: Significant multifamily supply incoming to Southwest Florida (Estero/Fort Myers submarket). The project's scale (600 units) and mixed-use density near Coconut Point signal developer confidence in demand elasticity in the region. Phase 1 delivery in Q3 2027 suggests near-term supply will compete with existing stock. Monitor absorption and rental rate trends in Estero/North Naples through 2027—early-phase ramp could accelerate rent growth or, if absorption lags, depress rents. Santander's $81.5M construction commitment reflects lender appetite for Florida multifamily, supporting continued development feasibility in the region.

stories.title: Alpharetta Mall May Convert to Mixed-Use Entertainment Center
stories.excerpt: The North Point Mall may be transformed into a sports-adjacent, mixed-use entertainment center. In a major move for professional sports in Georgia, the Alpharetta City Council voted to approve a vision to transform North Point Mall into a sports-adjacent, mixed-use entertainment district. Its all contingent on the NHL awarding a franchise team to the North Point site. The proposal, led by Jamestown on behalf of site owner New York Life and in partnership with Machete Group, includes a 20,000-seat NHL-ready arena, a 4,000-seat music hall and performing arts center, a 2,000-seat community hockey rink, a 1,100-seat movie theater, a 35,000-square-foot hotel conference center, and up to 650 rooms across two hotel buildings. The project also includes approximately 565,000 square feet of retail and dining, 750,000 square feet of office, 1,385 for-rent multifamily units, and more than 20 acres of publicly accessible parks, plazas and multi-use trails. The redevelopment is expected to be completed in phases, with various components opening on a rolling basis. The post Alpharetta Mall May Convert to Mixed-Use Entertainment Center appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: North Point Mall, Alpharetta, GA may convert to sports/mixed-use entertainment district
Conditional on NHL franchise award; Jamestown/New York Life proposal
1,385 for-rent multifamily units + 565K SF retail, 750K SF office, 2 hotels
stories.summary: Alpharetta City Council approved a vision to transform North Point Mall into a sports-adjacent mixed-use entertainment district, contingent on the NHL awarding a franchise to the site. Jamestown, on behalf of owner New York Life, in partnership with Machete Group, proposes a 20,000-seat NHL arena, 1,100-seat movie theater, 35,000 sq. ft. hotel conference center, two hotels (650 rooms), 1,385 for-rent multifamily units, 565,000 sq. ft. of retail/dining, 750,000 sq. ft. of office, and 20+ acres of parks. Phased rollout expected.
stories.impact: High-upside but contingent scenario for Atlanta North submarket (Alpharetta). If NHL franchise materializes, this project represents a catalyst for significant mixed-use infill redevelopment. The 1,385 multifamily units would add material supply to Alpharetta, but the NHL anchor and entertainment district design would likely drive strong demand—prime positioning for rents in the $1,800–$2,200/mo range for Class A product. Risk is high: without the NHL deal, the redevelopment stalls or scales down. Developers should monitor Alpharetta zoning/entitlement approvals and league signals closely before committing land or capital nearby.

stories.title: Law Firm Nutter Expands to 11K SF at Durst’s 5 Grand Central East
stories.excerpt: Law firm Nutter is taking more office space at one of the Durst Organization’s buildings near Grand Central Terminal, Commercial Observer has learned. Nutter, which is based in Boston and provides personal and business legal services, has signed a deal to renew its existing 5,719 square feet on the 27th floor of Durst’s 5 Grand Central East — also known as 655 Third Avenue — and add another 5,719 square feet on the entire 25th floor, according to the landlord. The deal brings the law firm’s total footprint at the 30-story office tower to 11,438 square feet. “The Manhattan office leasing market is surging, especially for Class A spaces in transit-accessible locations such as Grand Central East,” Jody Durst, president of Durst, said in a statement. “Nutter’s decision to expand at 5 Grand Central East reflects the desirability of the area and Durst’s long-term investment in our buildings.” The length of the lease was not provided, but the asking rent was $80 per square foot, according to Durst. CBRE’s Michael Joyce and Trevor Larkin brokered the deal for Nutter, while Durst was repped in-house by Tom Bow, Ashlea Aaron, Bailey Caliban and Sayo Kamara. A spokesperson for CBRE did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Nutter, which was founded in 1879, has been a tenant in Durst’s office building between East 41st and East 42nd streets since 2022. Michael Scott, co-managing partner of Nutter, said in a statement that 5 Grand Central East is “the right location for our clients and our team as we grow.” In December, Durst rebranded two of its office buildings near Grand Central, turning 655 Third Avenue to 5 Grand Central East and renaming 733 Third Avenue as 11 Grand Central East. The rebranding reflected its “continued investment in the Grand Central submarket,” the firm said. stories.summary: Law firm Nutter renewed and expanded its footprint at the Durst Organization's 5 Grand Central East (655 Third Avenue) in Manhattan, bringing total occupancy to 11,438 sq. ft. The deal renews Nutter's existing 5,719 sq. ft. on the 27th floor and adds the entire 25th floor (5,719 sq. ft.). Asking rent was $80 per sq. ft. Durst attributed the leasing activity to strong market demand for Class A office near Grand Central Terminal.
stories.impact: Limited direct multifamily impact. However, this signals stabilization in Manhattan's office market for Class A, transit-proximate space—a positive leading indicator for mixed-use and residential demand in Midtown. Office leasing momentum near Grand Central suggests commercial occupiers remain committed to Manhattan, supporting foot traffic and density for adjacent residential. Developers with mixed-use or residential projects in Midtown should monitor office tenant demand in the Grand Central/Murray Hill submarket as a proxy for neighborhood vitality and rent growth sustainability.

stories.title: Sheppard Takes 107K SF at In-Rel’s D.C. Redevelopment
stories.excerpt: One of the 50 highest-grossing law firms in the U.S. has signed an anchor lease at a planned Washington, D.C., trophy office redevelopment three years before its anticipated completion. Law firm Sheppard signed for 107,224 square feet at In-Rel Properties’ 2033 K Street NW, CBRE announced Tuesday. The firm, which has more than 1,200 attorneys across 16 offices, will move in after the building’s expected completion in July 2029. The brokerage did not disclose the value of the lease or the asking rent. In-Rel is expanding and updating the existing building, located along K Street near the intersection of D.C.’s Central Business District, West End and Dupont Circle. The developer will retain the property’s concrete structure while expanding it vertically and horizontally, including adding three floors and a penthouse. The renovations are another example of owners betting on Washington’s bifurcated office market, where distress coexists with a shortage of large, new trophy spaces, particularly for law firms and other high-end tenants. “We all know D.C. has plenty of office space, but what it doesn’t have is enough large-block, trophy-quality product that leading law firms like Sheppard demand,” In-Rel CEO Jackson Siegal said in a statement. Sheppard Chair Luca Salvi said the new office would provide a more modern and efficient workplace as the firm approaches its centennial and continues growing its Washington operation. CBRE’s Dimitri Hajimihalis, Emily Eppolito and Carroll Cavanagh represented In-Rel. Savills’ Gary Stein, David Lipson, Jon Glass and Owen Jaccard represented Sheppard. Gregory Cornfield can be reached at gcornfield@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Law firm Sheppard anchors 107K SF at In-Rel's 2033 K St NW, Washington DC
Move-in after July 2029 completion; In-Rel expanding/renovating existing structure
Firm ranked top 50 in U.S.; 1,200+ attorneys; 3-year lease pre-signature
stories.summary: Law firm Sheppard, one of the 50 highest-grossing U.S. law firms with 1,200+ attorneys across 16 offices, signed an anchor lease for 107,224 sq. ft. at In-Rel Properties' planned trophy redevelopment at 2033 K Street NW, Washington, D.C. The firm will move in after the building's anticipated July 2029 completion. In-Rel is expanding and updating the existing building by adding three floors and a penthouse. CBRE brokered the deal; lease terms and rent not disclosed.
stories.impact: Strong signal of pre-leasing traction and institutional demand for new Class A office in Washington's CBD/West End corridor. The 3-year advance anchor commitment de-risks In-Rel's redevelopment and validates trophy office scarcity in D.C.'s bifurcated market. For multifamily developers, this confirms continued flow of high-earning professional talent (law, finance, consulting) to D.C., supporting demand for luxury and high-end residential near K Street and central business district. Urban infill residential in D.C. with proximity to office clusters remains well-positioned for rent growth through 2029–2030.

stories.title: Eliot Spitzer Gains State Approval to Redevelop 985 Fifth Avenue After Legal Bout
stories.excerpt: Former New York Gov. Eliot Spitzer will finally get to demolish 985 Fifth Avenue after suing the state to obtain approval. Spitzer claimed that the state’s Division of Homes and Community Renewal (HCR) was delaying the approval of an application to not renew rent-stabilized leases in the building, a necessary step before the property could be redeveloped. Spitzer ultimately won the state’s blessing. The two-year request to end the rent-stabilized leases on the property followed approval from the New York City Landmarks Preservation Commission in 2023 to take a wrecking ball to the 25-story rental property and construct luxury condominiums in its place. Spitzer alleged potential misconduct in the lawsuit, reported by The Real Deal. Spitzer could not be reached for comment. HCR, now under the administration of Gov. Kathy Hochul, did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Spitzer’s Spitzer Enterprises has been advancing on other aspects of the project despite the delay, unveiling designs by SLCE Architects for the property in November 2025 which would yield 25 condo units, according to New York YIMBY. The former governor, who resigned in 2008 during a prostitution scandal, has owned the property since at least 2018 after buying seven residential buildings in the city, including 800 Fifth Avenue, with a total of 1.5 million square feet. Mark Hallum can be reached at mhallum@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Eliot Spitzer wins state approval to demolish 985 Fifth Avenue, Manhattan
Removes rent-stabilized lease barrier; Landmarks Preservation Commission approved 2023
Plan: luxury condo conversion; SLCE Architects design; 2-year HCR approval delay
stories.summary: Former New York Governor Eliot Spitzer obtained state approval to proceed with demolishing 985 Fifth Avenue (25-story rental building) after suing the state's Division of Homes and Community Renewal (HCR) to override delays in approving non-renewal of rent-stabilized leases. The New York City Landmarks Preservation Commission approved demolition in 2023; Spitzer Enterprises plans luxury condominium conversion. The state approval followed a two-year HCR delay and alleged potential misconduct in the approval process.
stories.impact: Limited impact on multifamily supply/demand (project converts rental to condos, net negative for rental stock). However, this signals potential weakening of rent-stabilization and leaseholder protections in New York City—a longer-term regulatory shift that could unlock more Manhattan rental-to-condo or mixed-use redevelopments. Developers with Manhattan development projects should monitor HCR administration and Landmarks approval timelines; this case suggests legal pressure and new governance may accelerate entitlement processes for high-value properties, opening windows for mid-sized rental redevelopments elsewhere on the Upper East Side and Central Park South.

stories.title: OCVibe Adds Five Dining Concepts to $5B SoCal District
stories.excerpt: The Samueli family has added five more dining concepts to the 50,000-square-foot market hall set to open next year as part of the $5 billion mixed-use development called OCVibe surrounding the Honda Center in Anaheim, Calif. Don Churros Gomez, MFK | Modern Filipino Kitchen, Mojo, Pull & Roll and Gelato Paradiso are the five new food options, adding Mexican, Filipino, Northern Chinese and Italian menus to the 21-kitchen market hall named Katella Commons. They join a growing roster at OCVibe, which earlier added concepts from chefs behind Amiga Amore, Burritos La Palma, Evil Cooks, Manaao Thai Comfort Food and Darkroom Restaurant and Wine Bar. Beloved Los Angeles chef Roy Choi is also bringing his Best Friend restaurant to the district. OCVibe did not disclose the values of the leases or the sizes of each space. Sources familiar with the development told Commercial Observer that OCVibe is fronting the initial investment, which averages around $300,000 per stall, as well as providing ongoing operational supports. “We wanted to approach this differently than a traditional landlord-tenant relationship,” OCVibe Senior Vice President Scott Frick said in a statement shared with CO. “Independent chefs are often asked to take on significant financial and operational risk before they ever serve their first meal. And unfortunately, many restaurants fail because of the significant upfront investment required of them.” Indeed, Frick recently told Commercial Observer that the Samueli family’s ownership structure has allowed the project to take a hands-on approach to restaurant leasing. Ownership is funding Katella Commons down to the kitchen equipment, allowing tenants to avoid substantial upfront costs of fitting out the new spaces. “Any tenant that comes in doesn’t have to come in with capital to fit out the kitchen — basically bring in your own knives and we’ll turn on the menu boards,” Frick said. bullets: OCVibe Samueli family adds 5 dining concepts to $5B Anaheim mixed-use district
Katella Commons market hall 50K SF opening next year; 21 kitchens total

stories.summary: The Samueli family added five new dining concepts—Don Churros Gomez, MFK (Filipino), Mojo (Northern Chinese), Pull & Roll, and Gelato Paradiso—to the 50,000 sq. ft. Katella Commons market hall opening in 2025 at OCVibe, the $5 billion mixed-use development surrounding the Honda Center in Anaheim, California. OCVibe is fronting approximately $300,000 per stall in initial investment and providing ongoing operational support. Celebrity chef Roy Choi's Best Friend restaurant is also coming to the district.
stories.impact: Demonstrates strong capital deployment and tenant recruitment momentum at a mega-scale mixed-use development. OCVibe's willingness to subsidize food-hall tenants (~$300K/stall) and absorb operational risk signals developer confidence in foot traffic and spend per visit—both dependent on proximate residential density and demand. The multifamily component of OCVibe (if any is planned) benefits from culinary and entertainment anchor tenants; conversely, nearby multifamily developments can capture spillover restaurant/entertainment demand. Monitor OCVibe's residential unit mix and lease-up timeline; strong retail and F&B execution will support rental rates for any Class A apartments within or adjacent to the district.
